chunks.text: In the classiﬁcation stage, feature-based systems ﬁrst extract the features and the performance of the classiﬁer is highly depen- dent on the feature extracted. The proper selection of feature extraction and classiﬁcation methods improves the detection rate. Haar-like features are composed of a number of black and white areas for which the intensities of the pixels in the black and white areas are calculated separately. The feature value is obtained using a weighted combination of the two values. Next, an adaboost detection algorithm is employed and then cascade classiﬁcation is used. Initial classiﬁers are used to remove most negative sam- ples. Next, classiﬁers that achieve low false positive error rates with increased computation are used. This cascade structure can take less time to achieve a high detection rate [6]. The most vulnerable pedestrians are those in the transportation system. Accurate detection of pedestrian trafﬁc is very important for computer vision in intelligent transportation systems and driver-assistance safety systems [7]. These pedestrian detection systems are usually single-camera based on a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) in which features based on Haar wavelet coefﬁcients are used to evaluate the classiﬁcation function. A similar structure is used for face and car detection that is not related to motion, tracking, background subtraction, or hypotheses based on the structure of the view [8]. The location of pedestrians can be determined using four examples based on the detectors. It then ensures that these mem- bers form the correct geometry based on classiﬁcation that catego- rizes the target object as humanoid. The results are better when the joined body is conﬁrmed [9]. Similar work has been done using stereo vision [10]. Some techniques are based on features such as similarity, the ﬁgure of the human body, or features of a vertical line [11,12]. Determination of pedestrian movement patterns using a SVM clas- siﬁcation function can also detect humans [13]. Researchers also use expensive hardware such as optical cameras, infrared cameras and conventional radar to provide real-time detection systems, but the use of these on automobiles is not generally cost-effective [14]. Networks of histogram of oriented gradient (HOG) descriptors using linear SVM classiﬁcation have good result in images that are to detect humans [15,16]. Humans can also be detected using an algorithm with low-level features to discriminate between pedestrians and non-pedestrians that can be further evaluated using an adaboost classiﬁer [17]. Some studies in this ﬁeld use a two-stage algorithm that employs a model for pedestrian detection based on machine vision. The ﬁrst step uses adaboost and cascade algorithms to segment the pedestrian from the image. The second stage removes errors to conﬁrm that each detected target is the image of the human. At this stage, SVM classiﬁcation evaluates pedestrian detection and input features using both grayscale and image-edge extraction, the results are better than one-stage classiﬁcations like adaboost or SVM [7]. These methods continue to show shortcomings in the application of machine vision to identify pedestrians. Advances in machine vision can be useful for this. The proposed DSWTS method is a ﬁve-stage algorithm, toward achieving this goal. We have named this algorithm as DSWTS by using ﬁrst letter of each stage (Division, Segmentation, Watershed techniques, Thresholding, Subtraction). To evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm under real conditions, a camera was installed on a tractor (MF399) (Fig. 1 ). Performance was tested at 30 km/h under morning, noon and evening lighting conditions and ﬁve distances between the human and tractor using four replications. The proposed algorithm was combined with the HOG method [5] and the cascade method [13], as two by two and also all three methods together. The results were compared two-by-two and for a combination of the three methods for mode of composition and performance of fusion algorithms. The number of treatments was 15 and the total num- ber of tests was 240. The results of the factorial completely ran- domized design were analyzed in SASv. 9.1 software. The results were compared for three indices: Accuracy: The number of frames that were correctly detected as human by the number of frames that were correctly detected as non-human divided by total number of frames.
